questions.stem: A data engineer needs to create and edit notebooks and pipelines in a workspace, but must not be able to grant anyone else access to it. Which workspace role fits?
options: Contributor
Member
Admin
Viewer
questions.explanation: Contributor is the role for people who build things: it allows creating and editing items in the workspace but not managing who else can get in. Member and Admin can both add other users, which is exactly what has to be withheld here, and Viewer cannot create anything at all.

questions.stem: An entire finance department of about ninety people needs Viewer access to a workspace, and the membership of that department changes every month. What should the role be granted to?
options: A Microsoft Entra security group that already contains the department
Each of the ninety users individually
The workspace app audience list
A sensitivity label applied to the workspace
questions.answer: A Microsoft Entra security group that already contains the department
questions.explanation: Workspace roles can be assigned to security groups, distribution lists and Microsoft 365 groups as well as to individuals. Binding the role to a group that is already maintained elsewhere means joiners and leavers are handled by whoever owns that group, rather than by someone remembering to edit a workspace. Naming ninety individuals works on day one and rots immediately.

questions.stem: You want a team lead to be able to add new analysts to a workspace as Contributors, without being able to delete the workspace itself. What is the lowest role that allows this?
options: Member
Contributor
Admin
Viewer
questions.explanation: Member can add other users to the workspace and reshare items, which covers adding analysts. Deleting the workspace and assigning the Admin role are reserved for Admin, so Member is the smallest grant that satisfies the requirement. Contributor cannot manage access at all.

questions.stem: An analyst from another team needs to read exactly one warehouse in a workspace that also holds twenty other items they must not see. What is the right way to grant that?
options: Share the warehouse item with them and give them no workspace role
Give them the Viewer role on the workspace
Give them the Contributor role and ask them not to open the rest
Move the warehouse into a new workspace for every such request
questions.answer: Share the warehouse item with them and give them no workspace role
questions.explanation: A workspace role applies to every item in the workspace, so Viewer would expose all twenty-one items. Item-level sharing grants access to a single item to someone who has no role in the workspace at all, which is precisely the granularity the requirement asks for.

questions.stem: A report author in a different workspace needs to create brand new reports on top of an existing semantic model, without being allowed to edit that model. Which permission do they need on it?
options: Build
Read
Write
Reshare
questions.explanation: Build permission is what allows a user to create new content on an existing semantic model: new reports, composite models, Analyze in Excel and XMLA read. Read alone lets someone open existing reports but not author against the model, and Write would let them change the model, which the requirement forbids.

questions.stem: A colleague already holds the Viewer role on a workspace, and you now want to stop them seeing one particular report in it. What actually achieves that?
options: Remove their workspace role and share only the items they should see
Add an explicit deny permission on that one report
Apply a sensitivity label to the report
Move the report to a folder inside the workspace
questions.answer: Remove their workspace role and share only the items they should see
questions.explanation: Workspace roles are additive and apply to the whole workspace; there is no per-item deny that overrides a role you have already granted. To exclude a single item you have to stop granting access at the workspace level and switch to item-level sharing. Labels classify and can protect content but do not remove a role, and folders organise rather than restrict.

questions.stem: Every regional manager opens the same report but must only see the rows for their own region. What do you configure in the semantic model to achieve that?
options: A security role containing a DAX filter expression on the region table
A page-level filter set to the region
A separate copy of the report for each region
A bookmark per region
questions.answer: A security role containing a DAX filter expression on the region table
questions.explanation: Row-level security is enforced in the model by defining roles whose DAX filter expressions restrict the rows a member of that role can see, and then assigning users to those roles. Filters and bookmarks live in the report and can be removed by anyone who can edit or export it, so they classify as convenience, not security.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Implement row-level, column-level, object-level, and file-level access control

questions.stem: A salary column must not merely be blank for most users, it must not appear in the field list at all. Which kind of access control does that?
options: Object-level security
Row-level security
A sensitivity label with encryption
Hiding the column in the model view
questions.explanation: Object-level security removes tables and columns from the model as far as an unauthorised user is concerned: the objects are not returned in metadata, so they cannot be listed or queried. Row-level security filters rows and leaves the column visible, and hiding a column in the model view is a tidiness setting that any user can reverse in their own view.

questions.stem: The same lakehouse table is read through the SQL analytics endpoint, through Spark notebooks and through a semantic model, and one row filter must apply identically to all three. Where should it be defined?
options: In OneLake security roles on the lakehouse itself
Separately in each semantic model that reads the table
In a view that every consumer is asked to use
In the workspace Viewer role
questions.answer: In OneLake security roles on the lakehouse itself
questions.explanation: Defining the restriction once at the data level in OneLake means every engine that reads the data enforces it, rather than each consumer reimplementing the same rule and one of them getting it wrong. Per-model roles have to be maintained in every model, and a view only helps for consumers who are disciplined enough to use it.

questions.stem: A semantic model carries a Highly Confidential sensitivity label, and someone now builds a new report on top of that model. What happens to the report?
options: It inherits the Highly Confidential label automatically
It is created with no label until someone applies one
It is blocked from being created
It inherits the label only if the author has the same clearance
questions.answer: It inherits the Highly Confidential label automatically
questions.explanation: Sensitivity labels flow downstream: content created from labelled content inherits the label, so classification follows the data instead of depending on the next author remembering to reapply it. That inheritance is the main reason labelling upstream items is worth the effort.

questions.stem: Data exported from a labelled report to an Excel file must stay unreadable to anyone outside the finance group, even after the file has left the tenant. What makes that true?
options: The label has encryption configured in its protection settings
The report is set to block export
The workspace is set to private
The semantic model has row-level security
questions.answer: The label has encryption configured in its protection settings
questions.explanation: A label with protection settings applies encryption and usage rights that travel with the file itself, so the restriction survives the export. Blocking export prevents the file existing at all rather than protecting one that does, and row-level security stops applying the moment data has been extracted into a workbook.

questions.stem: Your tenant needs a new sensitivity label called Restricted Research that Fabric users can apply to lakehouses and reports. Where is that label defined?
options: In Microsoft Purview, then published to users by a label policy
In the Fabric admin portal under tenant settings
In the workspace settings of each workspace
In the semantic model, as a model-level property
questions.answer: In Microsoft Purview, then published to users by a label policy
questions.explanation: Fabric consumes labels rather than defining them. The label taxonomy and its protection settings are created in Microsoft Purview Information Protection and published to users through a label policy; Fabric tenant settings only control whether labelling is switched on and how it behaves. Knowing which product owns which half of this is a common exam distinction.

questions.stem: A team wants to signal that their semantic model is ready for others to use, and any of them can apply the marking themselves. Which endorsement level is that?
options: Promoted
Certified
Master data
Featured
questions.explanation: Promoted is the self-service endorsement: anyone with write permission on the item can promote it, which makes it the right way for a team to say their own content is ready. Certification is deliberately not self-service, because a badge anyone can award means nothing.

questions.stem: Your organisation wants certification to mean something, so not everyone should be able to award it. Who decides which users may certify content?
options: The Fabric administrator, through a tenant setting that names the authorised users or groups
The owner of each individual item
Any workspace Admin, for their own workspace
Anyone who already holds a Certified item
questions.answer: The Fabric administrator, through a tenant setting that names the authorised users or groups
questions.explanation: Certification is restricted by a tenant setting in which an administrator lists the users or security groups permitted to certify. That central gate is the whole point of the level: promotion is self-service and cheap, certification is delegated to a named few and therefore carries weight.

questions.stem: A colleague argues that certifying a semantic model will let the rest of the company query it. Why is that wrong?
options: Endorsement affects discoverability and trust signals only, never permissions
Certification actually removes access until it is reviewed again
Certification grants access, but only to members of the same workspace
Endorsement grants access only after the next scheduled refresh
questions.answer: Endorsement affects discoverability and trust signals only, never permissions
questions.explanation: Endorsement is a quality signal: it adds a badge and lifts the item in the OneLake catalog and other discovery surfaces so people can find content worth using. It does not change who is allowed to read the item. Access still comes from workspace roles, item permissions and Build permission, and confusing the two leaves users able to see that something exists while being unable to open it.
